The document addresses the limitations of existing Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems, which often rely on flat data representations and lack contextual awareness, leading to fragmented and incoherent responses. Current RAG systems struggle to capture complex relationships between entities and adapt efficiently to new data. To overcome these challenges, the document proposes LightRAG, a new RAG system that integrates graph structures into text indexing and retrieval. LightRAG introduces a dual-level retrieval system—low-level for specific entity details and high-level for broader topics—and supports incremental updates to efficiently adapt to new information.

LightRAG enhances retrieval by segmenting documents into manageable pieces, extracting entities and relationships to form a knowledge graph, and using a dual-level retrieval paradigm to address both specific and abstract queries. The system also incorporates graph and vector-based retrieval to improve performance. Experimental evaluations on four datasets—Agriculture, CS, Legal, and Mix—demonstrate significant improvements over existing RAG methods. On the Agriculture dataset, LightRAG outperforms NaiveRAG by 67.6% in Comprehensiveness (p. 7), 76.4% in Diversity (p. 7), 67.6% in Empowerment (p. 7), and 67.6% in Overall (p. 7). Against RQ-RAG, it achieves 68.4% in Comprehensiveness (p. 7), 70.8% in Diversity (p. 7), 68.4% in Empowerment (p. 7), and 67.6% in Overall (p. 7). Against HyDE, it wins 74.0% in Comprehensiveness (p. 7), 76.0% in Diversity (p. 7), 74.8% in Empowerment (p. 7), and 75.2% in Overall (p. 7). Against GraphRAG, it achieves 54.4% in Comprehensiveness (p. 7), 77.2% in Diversity (p. 7), 58.8% in Empowerment (p. 7), and 54.8% in Overall (p. 7). In the Legal dataset, LightRAG achieves 83.6% in Comprehensiveness (p. 7), 86.4% in Diversity (p. 7), 83.6% in Empowerment (p. 7), and 84.8% in Overall (p. 7). Ablation studies show that removing either low-level or high-level retrieval leads to performance drops. LightRAG also demonstrates cost efficiency, using significantly fewer tokens and API calls than GraphRAG, such as fewer than 100 tokens for retrieval in the Legal dataset compared to 610,000 tokens for GraphRAG (p. 10).

LightRAG is a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system designed to enhance large language models (LLMs) by integrating external knowledge sources to provide more accurate and contextually relevant responses (p. 1). Existing RAG systems are limited by flat data representations and poor contextual awareness, leading to fragmented answers (p. 1). LightRAG addresses these issues by incorporating graph structures into text indexing and retrieval, enabling a dual-level retrieval system that improves information retrieval at both low and high levels of knowledge discovery (p. 1). The use of graph structures with vector representations allows for efficient retrieval of related entities and their relationships, improving response times while maintaining contextual relevance (p. 1). An incremental update algorithm ensures new data is integrated promptly, making the system effective in rapidly changing data environments (p. 1). Experimental validation shows significant improvements in retrieval accuracy and efficiency compared to existing approaches (p. 1). LightRAG is open-source and available at https://github.com/HKUDS/LightRAG (p. 1).

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems aim to improve large language models (LLMs) by incorporating external knowledge sources, as shown by Sudhi et al. (2024), Es et al. (2024), and Salemi & Zamani (2024). These systems allow LLMs to generate more accurate and contextually relevant responses, enhancing their real-world applicability. By adapting to domain-specific knowledge (Tu et al., 2024) and offering up-to-date information (Zhao et al., 2024), RAG systems tailor responses to user needs. Chunking, as noted by Lyu et al. (2024), is critical for breaking down text into manageable segments, improving retrieval accuracy and relevance.

Current RAG systems, however, face limitations. They often use flat data representations, which hinder their ability to capture complex relationships between entities. Additionally, they lack contextual awareness, leading to incoherent responses when dealing with interdependent topics (p. 1). For instance, a query about the influence of electric vehicles on air quality and public transportation might yield fragmented results due to the inability to synthesize information effectively (p. 1).

To overcome these issues, the authors propose integrating graph structures into RAG systems. Graphs effectively represent interdependencies among entities (Rampášek et al., 2022), enabling richer, more coherent responses. The proposed system, LightRAG, addresses three challenges: comprehensive information retrieval, enhanced retrieval efficiency, and rapid adaptation to new data (p. 2). LightRAG uses a dual-level retrieval framework—low-level for specific entity details and high-level for broader topics—combined with graph-based indexing to improve retrieval (p. 2). The system also supports incremental updates, reducing computational costs and enabling faster adaptation (p. 2). Experimental evaluations assessed LightRAG on retrieval accuracy, model ablation, response efficiency, and adaptability, showing significant improvements over baseline methods (p. 2).

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) combines user queries with relevant documents from an external knowledge database using two components: the Retrieval Component and the Generation Component (p. 2). The Retrieval Component fetches relevant documents based on the input query, while the Generation Component uses this retrieved information to generate contextually relevant responses (p. 2). The RAG framework is formally defined as M = (G, R = (φ, ψ)), where G is the generation module, R is the retrieval module, q is the input query, and D is the external database. The retrieval module R includes two functions: i) Data Indexer φ(·), which builds a data structure ˆD based on the external database D, and ii) Data Retriever ψ(·), which retrieves relevant documents by comparing the query with indexed data (p. 3). The generative model G(·) then uses the retrieved information and the initial query to produce high-quality responses (p. 3). The work emphasizes key aspects of an efficient RAG system: Comprehensive Information Retrieval, where the indexing function φ(·) must extract global information to enhance query answering (p. 3); Efficient and Low-Cost Retrieval, where the indexed data structure ˆD must allow rapid and cost-efficient retrieval for handling high query volumes (p. 3); and Fast Adaptation to Data Changes, where the system must quickly update the data structure to incorporate new information and remain current (p. 3).

LightRAG enhances retrieval by segmenting documents into manageable pieces and using LLMs to extract entities and relationships, forming a knowledge graph represented as ˆD = (ˆV, ˆE) = Dedupe ◦ Prof(V, E), V, E = ∪Di∈DRecog(Di) (p. 3). The process involves three steps: extracting entities and relationships via R(·), generating key-value pairs with P(·), and deduplicating via D(·) to reduce graph size and processing overhead (p. 3). This approach offers two advantages: comprehensive multi-hop subgraph understanding and enhanced retrieval performance through optimized key-value structures, outperforming embedding matching and chunk traversal (p. 4). LightRAG also supports fast adaptation to incremental knowledge bases by updating only new documents D′ using the same indexing steps φ, merging new ˆD′ = (ˆV ′, ˆE ′) with existing ˆD through union of node and edge sets (p. 4). The dual-level retrieval paradigm addresses specific and abstract queries using low-level (entity-focused) and high-level (topic-focused) retrieval strategies (p. 4). LightRAG integrates graph and vector-based retrieval, extracting local and global keywords, matching them in a vector database, and incorporating high-order relatedness via neighboring nodes {vi|vi ∈ V ∧(vi ∈ Nv ∨ vi ∈ Ne)} (p. 5). The answer generation phase uses retrieved information ψ(q; ˆD) and a general-purpose LLM to create answers from concatenated values of entities and relations (p. 5). Complexity analysis shows that the graph-based indexing phase requires LLM calls proportional to total tokenschunk size, with no additional overhead (p. 5). The retrieval phase uses LLM-based keyword generation and vector-based search for entities and relationships, reducing overhead compared to community-based traversal (p. 5).

The evaluation section of the document assesses the LightRAG framework against existing RAG methods using four datasets from the UltraDomain benchmark: Agriculture, CS, Legal, and Mix. These datasets range from 600,000 to 5,000,000 tokens. Questions are generated using an LLM to simulate real user tasks. LightRAG is compared to four baselines: NaiveRAG, RQ-RAG, HyDE, and GraphRAG. Evaluation is based on four dimensions: Comprehensiveness, Diversity, Empowerment, and Overall. For each dataset and each baseline, the win rate of LightRAG versus the baseline is reported. On the Agriculture dataset, LightRAG outperforms NaiveRAG by 67.6% in Comprehensiveness, 76.4% in Diversity, 67.6% in Empowerment, and 67.6% in Overall (p. 7). Against RQ-RAG, LightRAG wins 68.4% in Comprehensiveness, 70.8% in Diversity, 68.4% in Empowerment, and 67.6% in Overall (p. 7). Against HyDE, it achieves 74.0% in Comprehensiveness, 76.0% in Diversity, 74.8% in Empowerment, and 75.2% in Overall (p. 7). Against GraphRAG, LightRAG wins 54.4% in Comprehensiveness, 77.2% in Diversity, 58.8% in Empowerment, and 54.8% in Overall (p. 7). In the Legal dataset, the performance gap widens, with LightRAG achieving 83.6% in Comprehensiveness, 86.4% in Diversity, 83.6% in Empowerment, and 84.8% in Overall against other baselines (p. 7). Ablation studies show that removing either low-level or high-level retrieval leads to performance drops, while the full dual-level approach of LightRAG achieves balanced performance. The -Origin variant, which removes original text, does not show significant performance loss in some cases (p. 8). Case studies demonstrate that LightRAG provides more comprehensive, diverse, and empowering answers than GraphRAG in specific scenarios (p. 9). In terms of cost, LightRAG uses significantly fewer tokens and API calls than GraphRAG in both retrieval and incremental data update phases. For example, in the Legal dataset, LightRAG uses fewer than 100 tokens for retrieval, compared to 610,000 tokens for GraphRAG (p. 10). LightRAG also demonstrates superior adaptability to incremental data updates, avoiding the need to regenerate the entire community structure (p. 10).

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems enhance LLM inputs with external information to provide factually grounded responses (p. 10). Current RAG methods embed queries in vector space to find the nearest context vectors, but often rely on fragmented text chunks and only retrieve the top-k contexts, limiting their ability to capture comprehensive global information (p. 10). Recent studies have explored graph structures for knowledge representation, but these approaches often lack dynamic updates and expansions of the knowledge graph, making it difficult to incorporate new information effectively (p. 10). In contrast, the proposed LightRAG model enables the RAG system to adapt to new information, ensuring timeliness and accuracy (p. 10). Existing methods also rely on inefficient brute-force searches for each generated community, while LightRAG overcomes this with a dual-level retrieval paradigm, improving retrieval efficiency and response speed (p. 10). 

Graphs are a powerful framework for representing complex relationships, and researchers have focused on enhancing LLMs' ability to interpret graph-structured data (p. 10). This work is divided into three categories: i) GNNs as Prefix, where GNNs generate structure-aware tokens for LLMs during inference, as in GraphGPT and LLaGA (p. 10). ii) LLMs as Prefix, where LLMs process graph data to produce node embeddings or labels for refining GNN training, as in GALM and OFA (p. 10). iii) LLMs-Graphs Integration, which aims for seamless interaction between LLMs and graphs using fusion training, GNN alignment, and LLM-based agents, as in works by Li et al. and Brannon et al. (p. 10).

This work introduces an advancement in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) through the integration of a graph-based indexing approach that enhances both efficiency and comprehension in information retrieval (p. 10). LightRAG utilizes a comprehensive knowledge graph to facilitate rapid and relevant document retrieval, enabling a deeper understanding of complex queries (p. 10). Its dual-level retrieval paradigm allows for the extraction of both specific and abstract information, catering to diverse user needs (p. 10). Furthermore, LightRAG’s seamless incremental update capability ensures that the system remains current and responsive to new information, thereby maintaining its effectiveness over time (p. 10). Overall, LightRAG excels in both efficiency and effectiveness, significantly improving the speed and quality of information retrieval and generation while reducing costs for LLM inference (p. 10).

The Appendix of the document details the methodologies and experimental settings used in the LightRAG framework. It describes entity and relationship extraction from documents using large language models (LLMs), including the prompt templates and configurations for LLM operations. The evaluation criteria for assessing LightRAG against baselines are also outlined. Table 4 (p. 13) provides statistical information for four datasets: Agriculture (12 documents, 2,017,886 tokens), CS (10 documents, 2,306,535 tokens), Legal (94 documents, 5,081,069 tokens), and Mix (61 documents, 619,009 tokens). Figure 3 (p. 13) illustrates a retrieval-and-generate process for a sample query, where LLM extracts keywords and retrieves information structured into entities, relationships, and text chunks to generate a comprehensive answer. Figures 4-7 (p. 14–15) describe prompts for graph generation, query generation, keyword extraction, and RAG evaluation. The evaluation framework compares two answers based on Comprehensiveness, Diversity, and Empowerment. Table 5 (p. 16) presents a case study comparing LightRAG and NaiveRAG on a query about Indigenous perspectives on corporate mergers in Canada and Australia. LightRAG provides a more comprehensive, diverse, and empowering response, excelling in exploring cultural significance, collaboration, and legal frameworks. The LLM decision identifies LightRAG as the winner across all three evaluation criteria. The overall winner is Answer 2 (LightRAG) (p. 16).

The document introduces **LightRAG**, a novel Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system designed to address the limitations of existing RAG systems, which often rely on flat data representations and lack contextual awareness, leading to fragmented and incoherent responses [1]. LightRAG overcomes these challenges by integrating **graph structures** into text indexing and retrieval, enabling a **dual-level retrieval system**—low-level for specific entity details and high-level for broader topics [1]. This approach enhances the system's ability to capture complex relationships between entities and adapt efficiently to new data [1].

LightRAG improves retrieval performance by segmenting documents into manageable pieces, extracting entities and relationships to form a knowledge graph, and using graph and vector-based retrieval to address both specific and abstract queries [5]. The system supports **incremental updates**, allowing it to efficiently integrate new information without regenerating the entire knowledge structure [1]. 

Experimental evaluations on four datasets—**Agriculture**, **CS**, **Legal**, and **Mix**—demonstrate that LightRAG significantly outperforms existing RAG methods in terms of **Comprehensiveness**, **Diversity**, **Empowerment**, and **Overall** performance [6]. For instance, in the **Agriculture** dataset, LightRAG outperforms **NaiveRAG** by 67.6% in Comprehensiveness, 76.4% in Diversity, 67.6% in Empowerment, and 67.6% in Overall [6]. In the **Legal** dataset, the performance gap widens, with LightRAG achieving 83.6% in Comprehensiveness, 86.4% in Diversity, 83.6% in Empowerment, and 84.8% in Overall [6]. 

Ablation studies show that removing either low-level or high-level retrieval leads to performance drops, indicating the importance of the dual-level approach [6]. LightRAG also demonstrates **cost efficiency**, using significantly fewer tokens and API calls than competing systems like **GraphRAG**. For example, in the Legal dataset, LightRAG uses fewer than 100 tokens for retrieval, compared to 610,000 tokens for GraphRAG [6].

The document concludes that LightRAG enhances both **efficiency** and **effectiveness** in information retrieval and generation, significantly improving the speed and quality of responses while reducing computational costs [8]. It is open-source and available at [https://github.com/HKUDS/LightRAG](https://github.com/HKUDS/LightRAG) [2].
